about: T15 captions, written as a warm, clear tutor speaking; can be recorded as voiceover later. Times in seconds from the start of the lesson.

lines.text: Lesson fifteen: 1-minute, 5-minute and 15-minute timeframes.
Same market, grouped in different time windows.
Here are fifteen minutes of a fictional BTC chart, one candle per minute.
Tap 5m: now there are three candles. Tap 15m: just one.
Did the market change? No. Only the way it is grouped.
That grouping is called a timeframe.
A timeframe is how much time each candle covers.
On a 1-minute chart, each candle is one minute. On a 5-minute chart, five.
Like a diary: notes for each day, a summary each week, one for the month.
Same life, different summaries. Same trades, different candles.
Let's build one 5-minute candle from five 1-minute candles.
Open: the first minute's open. 60,000.
High: the highest high of all five. That is 60,110, in minute four.
Low: the lowest low of all five. 59,980, in the first minute.
Close: the last minute's close. 60,090.
Watch them merge: open 60,000, high 60,110, low 59,980, close 60,090.
It is green, because 60,090 closed above 60,000.
Fifteen minutes works the same way. Take all fifteen 1-minute candles.
First open, 60,000. Highest high, 60,170. Lowest low, 59,920.
Last close, 60,150. One green 15-minute candle.
The three 5-minute candles give the same answer. The maths always agrees.
Now one chart, one time axis. Under it all, the same price path.
Switch to 1-minute: fifteen narrow candles sit on the path.
Switch to 5-minute: they merge into three wider ones.
Switch to 15-minute: one candle for the whole stretch.
The path never moved. Only the grouping changed.
Short timeframes show every small back-and-forth. That is called noise.
On the 1-minute chart, 10:05 to 10:07 looks like a big drop.
On the 15-minute view, that drop is just a dip inside one green candle.
A signal is a change big enough to stand out from the noise. It is still no promise.
Higher-timeframe context: check the bigger view first.
Like a map: zoom out to see the city, then zoom in to find the street.
Look at 15m for the big picture, then 5m and 1m for detail.
If the views disagree, that is a reason to be careful, or to wait.
A common mistake: averaging the 1-minute highs to get the 5-minute high.
The average of these five highs is 60,060. That is wrong.
The 5-minute high is the highest of them: 60,120. Price really reached it.
Open is first, close is last, high is highest, low is lowest. No averages.
Your turn. Here are five 1-minute candles, from 10:10 to 10:14.
What are the 5-minute open, high, low and close? Pause if you need time.
Open 60,010, the first open. Close 60,150, the last close.
High 60,170, the highest high. Low 59,990, the lowest low.
A green 5-minute candle. Well done if you got all four.
Quick check: is each one a change in the view, or a real market event?
Switching timeframes and wider candles: just the view.
Trades and price moves are the market. The view only groups them.
Before we move on, a few honest limits.
Shorter timeframes are noisier. More candles do not mean more good chances.
Trading every small move piles up fees and mistakes.
No timeframe predicts the future. WAIT and NO_TRADE are always allowed.
Let's recap.
A timeframe is how much time each candle covers.
To combine candles: first open, highest high, lowest low, last close.
Check the bigger view for context. Short timeframes are noisy.
Check yourself: five 1-minute candles, the last closes at 60,090. The 5-minute close?
60,090. The 5-minute close is always the last 1-minute close.
Great work! Next up: trend and market structure.
See you in lesson sixteen.
